name: Design a Multi-Tenant SaaS Platform
intent: Serve thousands of customer organisations from shared infrastructure, so that each one feels alone on the system: its data is never visible to anyone else, a neighbour's burst does not slow it down, and the biggest customers can be given more isolation.
codeTitle: a tenant directory, row-level isolation and a fair queue
finalIntro: One request from a customer's employee, through to the metered bill.
prompt: Design a B2B SaaS product (invoicing, tickets, analytics, whatever it is) used by 5,000 customer organisations, called tenants, with 2 million users between them. A handful of tenants are huge, most are small, and a few need their data kept in a given country. One tenant must never be able to see another's data, and one tenant's heavy use must not slow down the others. Show how you route, isolate, migrate, customise and bill them.
functional: Every request belongs to exactly one tenant, found from the host name or the token
A tenant sees and changes only its own data
Tenants have their own settings, branding, feature flags and custom fields
Tenants are onboarded in seconds, and a large tenant can be moved to its own infrastructure
Usage is measured per tenant and turned into invoices
A tenant's data can be exported, restored and deleted on its own
nonFunctional: No cross-tenant data exposure, even if a developer makes a mistake in a query
A tenant at ten times its normal load must not push other tenants above their latency target
A failure or a bad query affects as few tenants as possible
Schema changes reach thousands of tenants without downtime, and can be rolled back or stopped half way
Data residency: a tenant's data stays in its chosen region
Cost per tenant stays low for the long tail of small tenants

firstAttempt.text: One application and one PostgreSQL database. Every table has a tenant_id column, and developers add 'where tenant_id = ?' to each query by hand, taking the tenant id from a field in the request. All customers use the same pool of servers.
limits: One forgotten 'where tenant_id' in thousands of queries shows one customer another's data, and nothing catches it
A tenant id taken from a request field can be changed by a user to someone else's
One tenant running a huge report or a burst of API calls slows every other tenant, and nobody can tell who
One database means one size limit, one outage for everyone and one migration that is all or nothing
No way to give a big or regulated customer its own database, region or limits, and no per-tenant usage numbers to bill

steps.title: Find the tenant on every request, and look it up in a directory
steps.problem: If the tenant id comes from a form field or a query parameter, any user can change it, and every other part of the system depends on knowing the tenant correctly.
steps.fix: A router at the edge decides the tenant once, from something the user cannot forge: the host name (globex.example.com or a verified custom domain) or the signed tenant claim in the access token, which must agree with each other. It then looks the tenant up in a tenant directory (a catalog): tenant id, shard (the database that holds the tenant's data), tier (pooled or dedicated), region, schema version, status and plan. The directory is small and read constantly, so every server keeps a cached copy that refreshes in a few seconds. The resolved tenant is put in a request context that is passed everywhere: the database session, the cache keys, the logs, the traces and the metrics.
steps.tradeoff: The tenant is known and trusted from the first hop, and moving or suspending a tenant is an edit to one row. The directory becomes a critical dependency, so it must be replicated and cached, and a cached copy can briefly point at an old shard after a move.

steps.title: Pool the small tenants on shared tables, and let the database enforce isolation
steps.problem: A database for every one of 5,000 tenants costs far too much for the small ones, but shared tables rely on every query remembering its filter.
steps.fix: Put the long tail of small tenants in pooled shards: shared tables with tenant_id as the first column of every primary key and index, so one tenant's rows are stored together and a lookup touches only them. Spread the tenants over a handful of shards, and let the directory say which. Turn on row-level security: each transaction starts by setting the tenant (SET LOCAL app.tenant = 'globex'), and a policy on every table says 'tenant_id = current_setting(app.tenant)'. The application connects as a role that does not own the tables and cannot bypass the policy, so even a query that forgets the filter returns only the caller's rows, and an insert with another tenant's id is rejected.
steps.tradeoff: The long tail costs a few dollars a month each, and there is one schema to migrate per shard. All the tenants on a shard share its CPU, its cache and its fate, and restoring one tenant means restoring a whole shard backup or exporting that tenant's rows. Database-per-tenant gives easy per-tenant restore but costs more and is slow to migrate, and schema-per-tenant makes the catalog huge: 5,000 schemas of 60 tables with 2 indexes each is 900,000 relations.

steps.title: Stop the noisy neighbour: limits, bulkheads and a fair queue
steps.problem: A pooled tenant that sends ten times its normal load, or runs a huge export, uses the shared capacity and every other tenant on the shard gets slow.
steps.fix: Every tenant is limited on its own: a token bucket per tenant (and per API key) at the edge sized by its plan (a counter that refills at a steady rate, where each request spends one token), a cap on concurrent requests, a cap on its database connections, a statement timeout, and quotas for storage and seats. Excess requests get a 429 (too many requests) with a Retry-After header that says when to try again. Background work goes to a job queue that is served fairly: one job per tenant in turn (or weighted by plan), so a tenant with 10,000 queued jobs cannot make a tenant with three wait behind them. Heavy work such as exports and reports runs on its own worker pool, a bulkhead, so it cannot take the threads that serve interactive requests. Per-tenant metrics show who is using what.
steps.tradeoff: One tenant's burst is turned into that tenant's own slowdown instead of everyone's. The limits need tuning, a legitimate burst from a good customer gets rejected until its plan or quota is raised, and limits do nothing for a bad query that is cheap to send and expensive to run, which needs the timeouts.

steps.title: Give the biggest customers their own shard, and be able to move any tenant
steps.problem: A tenant with 100 times the data of the average one, or with a contract that demands isolation, cannot share a shard: it dominates the capacity and its outage or bad query would hit its neighbours.
steps.fix: Tiers: most tenants are pooled, large or regulated ones are siloed, with their own shard (or a whole separate stack, in their own region or account). The code is identical, and only the directory entry points somewhere else. Moving a tenant between shards uses the same recipe each time: copy a snapshot of its rows to the target, stream the changes that happen meanwhile from the write-ahead log (the database's record of every change), pause its writes for a moment when the lag is near zero, check counts and checksums, flip the directory entry with a version number, resume, and delete the old copy after a retention period. The same mechanism rebalances shards and promotes a tenant that has outgrown the pool.
steps.tradeoff: Large customers get isolation, their own capacity and a smaller blast radius, and the platform can rebalance without downtime. Each silo costs real money and operations work, and every tier is one more shape of deployment to test, so the number of tiers is kept small.

steps.title: Migrate thousands of tenants, and customise without forking
steps.problem: A schema change has to reach every shard without downtime, and tenants want their own settings, fields and features without a separate code branch for each.
steps.fix: Schema changes use expand and contract: add the new column or table in a backward-compatible way, deploy code that works with both shapes, backfill in small batches, then remove the old shape later. A migration runner applies each step shard by shard in waves, small and internal tenants first, watches error rates, and stops on failure. The directory records the schema version of each shard so that the code can tell, and a half-migrated fleet is a normal state. Customisation lives in data, not code: per-tenant settings and branding, feature flags that can target a tenant or a plan, and custom fields stored as typed definitions with values in a JSON column or an extension table. Everyone runs the same build.
steps.tradeoff: One codebase and a gradual, stoppable migration, so a bad change is found on a few tenants rather than all of them. Code must support two schema versions at once, which makes migrations slower to finish, and custom fields are harder to index and report on than real columns.

steps.title: Meter usage per tenant, bill it, and keep data in its region
steps.problem: The business needs to know what each tenant used, in order to invoice it and to see the tenants that cost more than they pay, and some tenants require their data to stay in a country or region.
steps.fix: Every billable action (an API call, a seat-day, a gigabyte stored, a report run) emits a small event with the tenant id, a metric name, a quantity and a unique event id. The events go through a queue to an aggregator that writes de-duplicated totals per tenant per hour, and a billing job turns them into invoice lines using the tenant's plan. Storage and seats are sampled daily rather than sent as events. For residency, each tenant has a home region in the directory. Its data, backups, search index, logs and job queues are kept in cells in that region, the request is routed to that cell, and only a thin global control plane holds the directory and the billing totals, with no customer content.
steps.tradeoff: Invoices can be explained line by line, and cost per tenant is visible. Metering must never double count or lose events, so it needs idempotent writes (repeating one changes nothing) and reconciliation. Regional cells multiply the number of places to deploy and monitor, and a global feature such as cross-tenant search for support staff gets much harder.

failures.scenario: A developer forgets the tenant filter in a new report query
failures.impact: The report returns rows from every tenant on the shard, and one customer sees another's invoices. This is the worst possible failure for a SaaS product.
failures.answer: Row-level security is the last line of defence: the policy filters the query anyway, and the application role cannot bypass it (the table owner and superusers can, so the app must not use them). Other layers catch the bug earlier. All data access goes through a repository that takes the tenant context, a lint rule bans raw queries, and an automated test runs every endpoint as tenant A with tenant B's data present and fails if any B row comes back. Queries that return rows from more than one tenant raise an alert.

failures.scenario: A cache key does not include the tenant
failures.impact: A cached 'settings' or 'invoice list' entry written for one tenant is served to another that asks for the same key, which leaks data without any database bug.
failures.answer: Keys are built by one helper that always prefixes the tenant (t:globex:settings:v3), and the cache client refuses a key without it. The same applies to search indexes, file paths, queue names and metric labels. Per-tenant prefixes also allow one tenant's cache to be flushed or limited alone, and tests check that two tenants with the same object id get different entries.

failures.scenario: One tenant sends ten times its normal traffic
failures.impact: On a shared shard, the shared capacity fills, queues grow, and the small tenants next to it see multi-second latency or time out.
failures.answer: The per-tenant limiter turns the excess into 429 responses with Retry-After, the fair queue lets small tenants' jobs through between its jobs, and connection and statement limits stop it taking the database. Alerts name the tenant using the most capacity, and a tenant that regularly needs more is offered a higher plan or moved to a dedicated shard.

failures.impact: Every tenant on it is unavailable. With 500 tenants per shard that is 10% of customers from one failure.
failures.answer: The blast radius is chosen by the number of tenants per shard: fewer tenants per shard means more shards and more cost, but a smaller share of customers hit. Each shard has replicas and automatic failover, the router shows a clear status for affected tenants only, and the large and sensitive tenants are on dedicated shards so their availability does not depend on the pool. Error budgets are tracked per shard and per tier.

failures.scenario: A migration fails on 300 of 5,000 tenants
failures.impact: Some shards have the new schema and others do not, and the new code could break on the old ones.
failures.answer: The runner stops at the first failure in a wave, so the damage is limited to the early waves, and the directory shows which shard is on which version. The code always supports both the old and the new shape, so a half-migrated fleet works. The failed shards are retried or fixed by hand, and the contract step that removes the old shape waits until every shard is done.

alternatives.title: How tenants are isolated in the data layer

options.name: A database per tenant
options.pro: Strongest isolation, easy per-tenant backup, restore, export and delete, and no noisy neighbour at the data level
options.con: Highest cost for small tenants, thousands of connections and pools, and every migration runs thousands of times

options.name: A schema per tenant
options.pro: Cheaper than a database each, and a tenant can be moved with a schema dump
options.con: Huge catalogs (hundreds of thousands of tables and indexes), slow migrations and still a shared server

options.name: Shared tables with tenant_id and row-level security
options.pro: Cheapest and simplest to operate, one schema per shard, and onboarding is an insert
options.con: Isolation depends on policies being right, and per-tenant restore and noisy neighbours are harder

alternatives.pick: Shared tables with row-level security for the long tail, and a dedicated shard (or database) for large and regulated tenants. Database per tenant when there are few tenants and each is large.

alternatives.title: How the tenant is identified

options.name: A sub-domain or a verified custom domain
options.pro: Visible and hard to tamper with, and works before login
options.con: Needs wildcard certificates and domain verification

options.name: A claim in the signed token
options.pro: Works for APIs and mobile apps, and cannot be edited by the client
options.con: A user in several tenants needs a token per tenant, and revoking is hard

options.name: A header or a field sent by the client
options.con: Can be changed to another tenant's id, so it is only safe if checked against the token

alternatives.pick: The token claim is the authority for APIs, the host name for browsers, and the two must agree. Never trust a bare field.

alternatives.title: How noisy neighbours are contained

options.name: Rate limits and quotas per tenant
options.pro: Cheap, and works at the edge before any work is done
options.con: Only limits what it can count, and does not stop an expensive query

options.name: Fair queues and bulkheads
options.pro: Protect shared workers and pools whatever the cause
options.con: More moving parts, and the tenant's own work becomes slower

options.name: A dedicated shard for the heavy tenant
options.pro: Complete separation of capacity and failures
options.con: More cost, and a tenant can still overload itself

alternatives.pick: Limits and fair queues for everyone, plus a dedicated shard for the few tenants who need more.

alternatives.title: How big a pooled shard should be

options.name: Few shards with many tenants each
options.pro: Lowest cost and the least to operate
options.con: A failure or a bad query hits a large share of customers

options.name: Many shards with few tenants each
options.pro: Small blast radius and easy to move tenants
options.con: More cost, more migrations to run and more connections to manage

alternatives.pick: Choose from the blast radius you will accept. A shard of about 100 to 500 tenants means that one failure touches 2% to 10% of 5,000 customers.

roles.label: Router
roles.description: Finds the tenant and routes to its shard.

quiz.question: A SaaS product keeps all tenants in shared tables, and every query is supposed to end with 'where tenant_id = ?'. A developer ships a new report query without it, and review does not catch it. Which design makes sure the report still returns only the caller's rows?
options: A lint rule that bans raw SQL, combined with a checklist item in every code review for tenant filters
An ORM default scope that adds the tenant filter to every query that the application builds through the ORM
Putting the tenant id in the URL path of every endpoint, and checking it against the signed access token
Row-level security with the tenant set per transaction, and an application role that cannot bypass the policy
quiz.explanation: A database policy filters the rows whatever the query says, and a role without bypass rights cannot skip it. Lint rules, reviews and ORM scopes live in the application, so a raw query or a missed case slips past them, and the URL check only identifies the tenant, it does not filter rows.

quiz.question: There are 5,000 tenants, spread evenly over pooled shards. The business accepts that one shard failure may touch at most 2% of tenants, and wants as few shards as possible to keep cost down. How many pooled shards should the platform run?
quiz.explanation: 2% of 5,000 is 100 tenants, so a shard can hold at most 100, which means 50 shards. 10 and 20 shards would affect 10% and 5% of customers in one failure. 100 shards meet the limit too, but at double the cost of what the limit needs.

quiz.question: Tenant A stays within its rate limit of 100 requests per second, but each request starts a 40-second report on the shared database pool of 50 connections. The pool is full, and small tenants time out. Which change fixes the cause?
options: Cut every tenant's rate limit to 5 requests per second, so that fewer reports can start at the same time
Raise the pool from 50 to 200 connections, so that the reports have room and other tenants still get a connection
Add a per-tenant connection cap and statement timeout, and run reports on a separate pool fed by a fair queue
Move all 5,000 tenants to a database each, so no tenant can ever use a connection that belongs to another
quiz.explanation: The limiter counts requests, but the damage comes from long, expensive work, so concurrency caps, timeouts and a separate bulkhead pool contain it. A lower rate limit hurts good tenants and still lets a few reports fill the pool, and a bigger pool only moves the point where it fills. A database for every tenant removes the shared pool but multiplies cost and migrations by 5,000, and a tenant still overloads its own database.
